newsitem.title: GREECE: Bankers see Greek/BTP yield gap wider by end-97.
newsitem.headline: Bankers see Greek/BTP yield gap wider by end-97.

text.p: Market jitters about Greece's economic performance over the next few months and a rising cost of carry have blown the froth off its bond market and bankers predict a wider Greek/BTP yield gap by end-97.

"I expect the spread of Greece's 10-year bond over BTP to widen more in the next few months," said a treasurer at a foreign bank. "About half of it will be accounted for by lower BTP yields and the rest by a rise in Greek yields."
The 10-year Greek-BTP yield spread bloated to 312 basis points on Thursday from 232 basis points on July 1.

Higher funding costs on tighter liquidity and a heavier-than-expected state borrowing schedule reinforced bearish sentiment and took their toll on Greek bonds. EMU-linked euphoria accounted for a rally in BTPs.
Other bankers agreed that a widening of the Greek-BTP yield spread was on the cards by end-1997.

"If anything, a further widening of 50 to 100 basis points in the yield spread between Greece's 10-year bond and the BTP should be expected by end-97," said Richard Bruens, treasurer at ABN-AMRO Bank, Athens. "Greek yields are still low."
Asked what was a fair yield for the 10-year bond, Bruens said it should be definitely above 10 percent.

All bankers cited difficulties in reducing inflation, reforming public finances and reversing the deteriorating trend in the current account deficit as the main reasons behind a pick-up in Greek bond yields.
Some bankers said foreign investors would go for Greece's 10-year high yielder if its spread over the BTP ballooned to over 350 basis points.

"With inflation difficult to cut below 5.5 percent, concerns about the attainment of the budget deficit target and a deteriorating current account balance, it is hard to see how foreign investors can be lured into the Greek 10-year bond with spreads below 350," he said.
A downward sloping treasury yield curve is justified up to the end of 2001 but risk premia are large enough and should be incorporated in yields thereafter, said the treasurer of ABN AMRO Bank.

"The market takes a big bet on positive economic and political developments with a downward sloping yield curve extending to 10-years," he added. "I do believe Greece will make it to the EMU by end-2001 but no one can be sure about it."
Greece hopes to join the second wave of EMU by the end of 2001 at the latest but has yet to satisfy a single Maastricht criterion despite making considerable progress on many fronts.
CPI-based inflation was running at 5.5 percent year-on-year in June, down from 8.4 percent year-on-year in the same month a year ago.
National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou told reporters on Wednesday that bringing inflation below 3.0 percent in 1998 would be a top economic policy priority.
The general government budget deficit is projected to drop to 4.2 percent of GDP this year from 7.4 percent in 1996. Greece's EU-approved convergence plan calls for a ratio of 2.4 percent in 1998.

Asked if an improvement in the infrastructure and functioning of Greece's secondary bond market would justify lower yield spreads even under stagnating macroeconomic fundamentals, the bankers said it would help them narrow.

"If the primary dealers group is finally set up and the central bank's electronic trading system starts operating, the secondary bond market will have more depth and improve liquidity," said Harris Makkas, country treasurer at Bank of America.
"This will help push Greek yields down and save the state lots of money."

Greece's secondary bond market got a boost when banks started quoted prices on Reuters multicontributor pages. In another positive development, Euroclear services will be offered for Greek domestic debt securities from August 4.
Greeces' domestic debt was rated for the first time ever this year.
Other bankers said the setting up of the primary dealers group would lead to a flourishing forward market in government securities as well as a well-functioning repo market.

Introduction of regular auctions of 12-month T-bills, which are used to refix coupons on Greece's drachma floating rate notes, would also contribute to the smooth functioning of the state securities market and increase participation by the market's foreign component.
"The state should start auctioning T-bills regularly to eliminate the basis risk inherent under the current setting," said a senior banker at another foreign bank.
Apart from on one occasion Greece has always set 12-month T-bill rates administratively. -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
